events.title: The death of Pope St. Gregory the Great
events.shortBlurb: The monk-pope who reformed the liturgy, sent missionaries to England, and called himself “servant of the servants of God” died in Rome…
body: Born at Rome about 540, son of the patrician Gordianus and the sainted Silvia, Gregory was prefect of the city about 573; renouncing the world, he founded six monasteries on his Sicilian estates and made his father's house on the Caelian Hill a seventh, St Andrew's, where he took the cowl.

Drawn from the cloister to serve as deacon and then as papal ambassador at Constantinople, he was chosen pope in 590 when plague carried off Pelagius II, and consecrated on 3 September. He fed Rome's poor from the Church's patrimony, made peace with the Lombards, and reformed the Roman liturgy and the chant that bears his name.

His Pastoral Rule, his Moralia on Job, his Dialogues, and his homilies formed the medieval Church; and in 596 he sent Augustine of Canterbury and his monks to preach the Gospel to the English. He styled himself 'servant of the servants of God', the title the popes bear still.

Worn by gout and labor, he died on 12 March 604 and was buried in the portico of St Peter's, acclaimed a saint at once. A Doctor of the Church, his feast is now kept on 3 September, the day of his consecration.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Gregory I (the Great)”

events.title: The canonizations of 1622
events.shortBlurb: On a single day Pope Gregory XV raised Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, Philip Neri, and Isidore to the altars…
body: On 12 March 1622 Gregory XV raised five blesseds to the altars in St Peter's, the first time five saints were proclaimed together: Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Society of Jesus; Francis Xavier, its missionary to India and Japan; Teresa of Ávila, reformer of Carmel; Philip Neri, founder of the Oratory and apostle of Rome; and Isidore, a farm laborer of Madrid dead nearly five hundred years.

The five crowned the Catholic renewal that followed the Council of Trent: the new religious orders, the missions overseas, the mystical reform of prayer, and the holiness of ordinary lay life. Spain, which claimed four of the five, bore most of the cost of the festivities, and Isidore's place among them made the day a triumph for Madrid as much as for Rome.

Roman wit had its say through Pasquino, the talking statue: the pope, it observed, had canonized four Spaniards and a saint, Philip Neri being the only Italian. The jest was long remembered; so was the day itself, which fixed the model of the great shared canonizations held at Rome ever since.
